claim: Peptidoglycan (PG) is the main component of bacterial cell walls and the target for many antibiotics.
source: Peptidoglycan (PG) is the main component of bacterial cell walls and the target for many antibiotics.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in microbiology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: PG biosynthesis is tightly coordinated with cell wall growth and turnover.
source: PG biosynthesis is tightly coordinated with cell wall growth and turnover
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about bacterial cell wall biology.

claim: Many control activities of PG biosynthesis depend upon PASTA-domain containing eukaryotic-like serine/threonine protein kinases (PASTA-eSTK) that sense PG fragments.
source: many of these control activities depend upon PASTA-domain containing eukaryotic-like serine/threonine protein kinases (PASTA-eSTK) that sense PG fragments.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field of bacterial cell wall regulation.

claim: Only a few PG biosynthetic enzymes are direct kinase substrates.
source: However, only a few PG biosynthetic enzymes are direct kinase substrates.
evidence: This statement is based on the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: ReoM protein is a novel PASTA-eSTK substrate in Listeria monocytogenes.
source: Here, we identify the conserved ReoM protein as a novel PASTA-eSTK substrate in the Gram-positive pathogen Listeria monocytogenes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The phosphorylation of ReoM is essential.
source: Our data show that the phosphorylation of ReoM is essential
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that the T7A mutation in ReoM is lethal.

claim: ReoM phosphorylation controls ClpCP-dependent proteolytic degradation of MurA.
source: Our data show that the phosphorylation of ReoM is essential as it controls ClpCP-dependent proteolytic degradation of the essential enzyme MurA
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MurA accumulation in various mutants and degradation assays.

claim: MurA catalyses the first committed step in PG biosynthesis.
source: the essential enzyme MurA, which catalyses the first committed step in PG biosynthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MurA function in bacterial cell wall biosynthesis.

claim: ReoY is a second novel factor required for degradation of ClpCP substrates.
source: We also identify ReoY as a second novel factor required for degradation of ClpCP substrates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing MurA accumulation in ΔreoY mutants.

claim: The first committed step of PG biosynthesis is activated through control of ClpCP protease activity in response to signals of PG homeostasis imbalance.
source: Collectively, our data imply that the first committed step of PG biosynthesis is activated through control of ClpCP protease activity in response to signals of PG homeostasis imbalance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and represents an inference about the biological mechanism.

claim: The cell wall of Gram-positive bacteria is a complicated three-dimensional structure that engulfs the cell as a closed sacculus.
source: The cell wall of Gram-positive bacteria is a complicated three-dimensional structure that engulfs the cell as a closed sacculus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial cell wall structure.

claim: PG biosynthesis starts with the conversion of UDP-GlcNAc into lipid II.
source: PG biosynthesis starts with the conversion of UDP-GlcNAc into lipid II, a disaccharide pentapeptide that is ligated to a membrane-embedded bactoprenol carrier lipid (Typas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Lipid II is flipped from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane by MurJ- and Amj-like enzymes called flippases.
source: This monomeric PG precursor is then flipped from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane by MurJ- and Amj-like enzymes called flippases (Ruiz, 2008; Sham et al., 2014; Meeske et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Glycosyltransferases belonging to bifunctional penicillin binding proteins (PBPs) or the SEDS family transfer disaccharide pentapeptides to growing PG strands.
source: Glycosyltransferases belonging either to the bifunctional penicillin binding proteins (PBPs) or the SEDS (shape, elongation, division and sporulation) family then transfer the disaccharide pentapeptides to growing PG strands
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: PG strands are crosslinked by a transpeptidation reaction catalysed by bifunctional (class A) or monofunctional (class B) PBPs.
source: which are finally crosslinked by a transpeptidation reaction catalysed by bifunctional (class A) or monofunctional (class B) PBPs (Sauvage et al., 2008; Meeske et al., 2016; Emami et al., 2017; Taguchi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: PASTA-eSTKs are stimulated by free muropeptides and lipid II that accumulate during damage and turnover of PG.
source: These proteins are stimulated by free muropeptides and lipid II (that accumulate during damage and turnover of PG) on interaction with their PASTA domains (Mir et al., 2011; Hardt et al., 2017; Kaur et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: PknB phosphorylates GlmU, reducing GlmU activity.
source: PknB, a representative PASTA-eSTK from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, phosphorylates GlmU, a bifunctional uridyltransferase/acetyltransferase important for synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc, and in so doing reduces GlmU activity (Parikh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: M. tuberculosis MviN is a substrate of PknB.
source: M. tuberculosis MviN, a MurJ-like flippase, is also a substrate of PknB
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Phosphorylated MviN (P-MviN) is inhibited by its binding partner FhaA.
source: and, in its phosphorylated state, P-MviN is inhibited by its binding partner, FhaA (Gee et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: M. tuberculosis PknB phosphorylates the class A PBP PonA1.
source: M. tuberculosis PknB also phosphorylates both the class A PBP PonA1 (Kieser et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: M. tuberculosis PknB phosphorylates the amidase-like protein CwlM, which is essential for growth.
source: and the amidase-like protein CwlM, which is essential for growth (Deng et al., 2005; Boutte et al., 2016; Turapov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: CwlM is membrane-associated and interacts with MurJ to control lipid II export.
source: CwlM is membrane-associated and interacts with MurJ to control lipid II export (Turapov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: When phosphorylated, P-CwlM re-locates from the membrane to the cytoplasm.
source: However, when phosphorylated, P-CwlM re-locates from the membrane to the cytoplasm (Turapov et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: P-CwlM allosterically activates MurA 20–40-fold.
source: where it allosterically activates MurA 20–40-fold (Boutte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: MurA catalyzes the first committed step of PG biosynthesis by transferring an enoylpyruvate moiety to UDP-GlcNAc.
source: MurA catalyzes the first committed step of PG biosynthesis by transferring an enoylpyruvate moiety to UDP-GlcNAc
evidence: This is established knowledge about MurA function.

claim: MurA is essential in M. tuberculosis and in many other bacterial species tested.
source: MurA is essential in M. tuberculosis and in many other bacterial species tested (Brown et al., 1995; Kock et al., 2004; Griffin et al., 2011; Rismondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The L. monocytogenes PASTA-eSTK, PrkA, phosphorylates YvcK.
source: Finally, the Listeria monocytogenes PASTA-eSTK, PrkA, phosphorylates YvcK, which is required for cell wall homeostasis in a so far unknown way (Pensinger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: GpsB from L. monocytogenes is important for the last two steps of PG biosynthesis (transglycosylation and transpeptidation).
source: We have shown previously that GpsB from L. monocytogenes is important for the last two steps of PG biosynthesis, i. e. transglycosylation and transpeptidation, by providing an assembly platform for the class A PBP, PBP A1 (Rismondo et al., 2016; Cleverley et al., 2016; Cleverley et al., 2019; Halbedel and Lewis, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors and others.

claim: The adaptor function of GpsB is maintained in at least B. subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: and this adaptor function of GpsB is maintained in at least B. subtilis and Streptococcus pneumoniae (Cleverley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: An L. monocytogenes ΔgpsB mutant is impaired in PG biosynthesis and cannot grow at elevated temperatures.
source: An L. monocytogenes ΔgpsB mutant is impaired in PG biosynthesis and cannot grow at elevated temperatures (Rismondo et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The ΔgpsB phenotype is readily corrected by a suppressor mutation in clpC.
source: but this phenotype is readily corrected by a suppressor mutation, which mapped to clpC (Rismondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: ClpC is the ATPase subunit of the ClpCP protease that degrades substrate proteins upon heat stress.
source: ClpC is the ATPase subunit of the ClpCP protease that degrades substrate proteins upon heat stress (Molière and Turgay, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: MurA is a ClpCP substrate in both B. subtilis and L. monocytogenes.
source: MurA (aka MurAA in B. subtilis) is a ClpCP substrate in both B. subtilis and L. monocytogenes (Kock et al., 2004; Rismondo et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: MurA strongly accumulates in a L. monocytogenes ΔclpC mutant.
source: and strongly accumulates in a L. monocytogenes ΔclpC mutant (Rismondo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A deficiency in the final two enzymatic steps of PG biosynthesis in the absence of GpsB is corrected by mutations in clpC that increase the amount of MurA.
source: Thus, a deficiency in the final two enzymatic steps of PG biosynthesis in the absence of GpsB is corrected by mutations in clpC that increase the amount of the first enzyme of the same PG biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript and previous work.

claim: Three shg suppressor mutants (shg8, shg10, and shg12) were isolated from a ΔgpsB mutant incubated at 42°C.
source: We have characterised three more shg (suppression of heat sensitive growth) suppressor mutants (shg8, shg10 and shg12) isolated from a ΔgpsB mutant incubated on a BHI agar plate at 42°C.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure and results.

claim: The three shg strains grew as fast as the wild type when cultivated at 37°C or 42°C.
source: These three shg strains grew as fast as the wild type when cultivated at 37°C or 42°C
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The parental ΔgpsB mutant grew at a reduced rate at 37°C and did not grow at 42°C.
source: whereas the parental ΔgpsB mutant grew at a reduced rate at 37°C and did not grow at 42°C (Figure 1A–B), as shown previously (Rismondo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1A-B and a citation to previous work.

claim: Strain shg8 carried a mutation in the lmo1921 gene (reoY) that exchanged H87 into tyrosine.
source: Strain shg8 carried a mutation in the uncharacterized lmo1921 gene (herein named reoY, see below) that exchanged H87 into tyrosine
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data.

claim: Strain shg10 carried a mutation in reoY that introduced a premature stop codon after the 73rd codon.
source: the same gene was affected by the introduction of a premature stop codon after the 73rd reoY codon in strain shg10.
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data.

claim: Strain shg12 carried a mutation in the ribosomal binding site (RBS) of the lmo1503 gene (reoM).
source: Strain shg12 carried a mutation in the ribosomal binding site (RBS) of the lmo1503 gene (renamed reoM), encoding an IreB-like protein
evidence: This is based on genome sequencing data.

claim: Deletion of reoM had no effect on growth of wild type bacteria.
source: While deletion of reoM had no effect on growth of wild type bacteria
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Deletion of reoM completely suppressed the growth defects of the ΔgpsB mutant at both 37°C and 42°C.
source: it completely suppressed the growth defects of the ΔgpsB mutant at both 37°C and 42°C (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: The mutation in the reoM RBS in strain shg12 likely impairs reoM expression.
source: It is thus likely that the mutation in the reoM RBS impairs its expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of reoM suppresses the ΔgpsB phenotype.

claim: Deletion of reoY completely restored growth of the ΔgpsB mutant at both 37°C and 42°C.
source: Likewise, deletion of reoY completely restored growth of the ΔgpsB mutant at both temperatures (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Expression of an additional copy of reoM impaired growth of the ΔgpsB mutant without affecting the growth of wild type bacteria.
source: Expression of an additional copy of reoM impaired growth of the ΔgpsB mutant without affecting the growth of wild type bacteria
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of a second copy of reoY had no effect on growth.
source: whilst expression of a second copy of reoY had no effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The expression of reoM is inversely correlated with the growth of the ΔgpsB mutant.
source: The expression of reoM is thus inversely correlated with the growth of the ΔgpsB mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that overexpression of reoM impairs growth of the ΔgpsB mutant while deletion of reoM suppresses the growth defect.

claim: The cell lengths of ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants were wild type-like and unaffected by the presence or absence of gpsB.
source: their cell lengths were wild type-like and unaffected by the presence or absence of gpsB, suggesting the absence of cell division defects in the ΔreoM or ΔreoY mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the cell length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: ΔreoM and ΔreoY single mutants had a normal rod-shape.
source: Scanning electron micrographs of ΔreoM and ΔreoY single mutants revealed that these bacteria had a normal rod-shape
evidence: This is supported by the scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The ΔgpsB ΔreoM and ΔgpsB ΔreoY double mutants were partially bent.
source: but that the ΔgpsB ΔreoM and ΔgpsB ΔreoY double mutants were partially bent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), implying the presence of some shape maintenance defects along the lateral cell cylinders.
evidence: This is supported by the scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: MurA accumulated by at least eight-fold in ΔreoM or ΔreoY mutants compared to the wild type.
source: MurA accumulated by at least eight-fold in comparison to the wild type in the absence of reoM or reoY (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MurA levels in ΔreoM or ΔreoY mutants reached similar levels to a mutant lacking clpC.
source: and reached similar levels to a mutant lacking clpC, which encodes the ATPase subunit of the ClpCP protease (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MurAA is degraded by the ClpCP protease in vivo in B. subtilis.
source: MurAA, the B. subtilis MurA homologue, is degraded by the ClpCP protease in vivo (Kock et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The MurA levels in ΔclpC, ΔreoM and ΔreoY single mutants were the same as in ΔclpC ΔreoM and ΔclpC ΔreoY double mutant strains.
source: The MurA levels in ΔclpC, ΔreoM and ΔreoY single mutants were the same as in ΔclpC ΔreoM and ΔclpC ΔreoY double mutant strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The MurA level in a mutant lacking murZ is not additive to the MurA level in ΔclpC cells.
source: Likewise, the MurA level in a mutant lacking murZ, previously shown to contribute to MurA accumulation (Rismondo et al., 2017), is not additive to the MurA level in ΔclpC cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to previous work.

claim: ReoM, ReoY and MurZ likely affect the ClpCP-dependent degradation of MurA.
source: Therefore, ReoM, ReoY and MurZ likely affect the ClpCP-dependent degradation of MurA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MurA levels in mutants lacking these genes are not additive to the MurA level in ΔclpC cells.

claim: Combinations of ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ deletions did not exert any additive effect on accumulation of MurA.
source: Combinations of ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ deletions did also not exert any additive effect on accumulation of MurA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ReoM, ReoY and MurZ all belong to the same pathway.
source: further validating the conclusion that these genes all belong to the same pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that combinations of deletions do not have additive effects.

claim: MurA was almost completely degraded in wild type cells 80 min after chloramphenicol treatment.
source: MurA was almost completely degraded in wild type cells 80 min after chloramphenicol treatment (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: DivIVA was stable after chloramphenicol treatment.
source: whereas DivIVA was stable (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No MurA degradation was observed in mutants lacking clpC, reoM or reoY.
source: By contrast, no MurA degradation was observed in mutants lacking clpC, reoM or reoY (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ReoM and ReoY are as important for MurA degradation as is ClpC.
source: which together demonstrates that ReoM and ReoY are as important for MurA degradation as is ClpC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MurA is not degraded in mutants lacking reoM or reoY.

claim: Homologues of the 90-residue ReoM protein are found across the entire Firmicute phylum.
source: Homologues of the 90-residue ReoM protein are found across the entire Firmicute phylum
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ReoM homologues include IreB from Enterococcus faecalis.
source: and include IreB, a substrate of the protein serine/threonine kinase IreK and its cognate phosphatase IreP from Enterococcus faecalis (Hall et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: ReoY homologues are present only in the Bacilli.
source: whereas ReoY homologues are present only in the Bacilli.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: A reoY homologue has been identified as a ΔireK suppressor in E. faecalis.
source: A reoY homologue has been identified as a ΔireK suppressor in E. faecalis (Banla et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The function of the E. faecalis reoY and reoM homologues remains unknown.
source: but the function of the E. faecalis reoY and reoM homologues remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In B. subtilis, ReoM corresponds to YrzL and ReoY to YpiB.
source: In B. subtilis, ReoM corresponds to YrzL (e-value 3e−29) and ReoY to YpiB (4e−61)
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis.

claim: MurAA accumulated by at least 12-fold in B. subtilis ΔyrzL and ΔypiB mutants compared to the wild type.
source: MurAA accumulated by at least 12-fold in these strains in comparison to the wild type.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The amount of MurAA was increased by 12-fold in the B. subtilis ΔclpC mutant.
source: Furthermore, the amount of MurAA was also increased by 12-fold in the ΔclpC mutant.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ReoM and ReoY functions are conserved in L. monocytogenes and B. subtilis.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that ReoM and ReoY functions are conserved in both species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of the homologous genes in B. subtilis has similar effects on MurAA levels.

claim: The levels of GlmS and IlvB were significantly increased in B. subtilis ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants.
source: The levels of both proteins were also significantly increased in B. subtilis ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: ReoM and ReoY are required for degradation of ClpC substrates in general.
source: indicating that ReoM and ReoY are required for degradation of ClpC substrates in general.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple ClpC substrates accumulate in ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants.

claim: Artificial overproduction of MurA in strain LMJR116 led to a 12-fold increase of ceftriaxone resistance.
source: Artificial overproduction of MurA in strain LMJR116, which carries an IPTG-inducible murA gene in addition to the native copy on the chromosome, lead to a 12-fold increase of ceftriaxone resistance
evidence: This is supported by the MIC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MurA depletion lowered ceftriaxone resistance.
source: while MurA depletion lowered ceftriaxone resistance (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the MIC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MurA levels are directly correlated with PG production.
source: MurA levels are thus directly correlated with PG production, presumably leading to stimulation or impairment of PG biosynthesis during overproduction and depletion, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that MurA levels correlate with ceftriaxone resistance.

claim: Ceftriaxone resistance of the ΔclpC mutant increased to the same degree as when MurA was overproduced.
source: In good agreement with the overproduction of MurA, ceftriaxone resistance of the ΔclpC mutant increased to the same degree as when MurA was overproduced (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the MIC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ceftriaxone resistance of ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants increased two- to three-fold.
source: Ceftriaxone resistance of ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants increased two- to three-fold (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by the MIC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The intermediate ceftriaxone resistance level in ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants is probably explained by the presence of functional ClpCP in these strains.
source: this intermediate resistance level is probably explained by the presence of functional ClpCP in these strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the resistance level is lower than in the ΔclpC mutant.

claim: Thicker PG layers were observed at the cell poles of ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants.
source: In good agreement with this concept of stimulated PG biosynthesis during MurA accumulation, we observed thicker PG layers at the cell poles of ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants
evidence: This is supported by the transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔreoM and ΔreoY mutants have more uneven PG layers along their lateral wall.
source: which also have more uneven PG layers along their lateral wall, whereas both phenomena were not observed in wild type cells (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants showed salt-sensitive growth.
source: Moreover, ΔreoM, ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants showed salt-sensitive growth (Figure 3C)
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Salt sensitivity is a known phenotype of the L. monocytogenes ΔclpC mutant.
source: which is a known phenotype of the L. monocytogenes ΔclpC mutant (Rouquette et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Salt sensitivity of the ΔreoM mutant was as severe as for the ΔclpC mutant.
source: Salt sensitivity of the ΔreoM mutant was as severe as for the ΔclpC mutant
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants showed milder salt sensitivity phenotypes than the ΔreoM mutant.
source: whereas the ΔreoY and ΔmurZ mutants showed milder phenotypes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the growth curves shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Modulation of MurA levels effectively controls PG biosynthesis.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that modulation of MurA levels effectively controls PG biosynthesis
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations that MurA levels correlate with ceftriaxone resistance, PG thickness, and salt sensitivity.

claim: ReoM, ReoY and MurZ play an important role in regulation of PG biosynthesis.
source: and also demonstrate that ReoM, ReoY and MurZ play an important role in its regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations that deletion of these genes affects MurA levels and PG biosynthesis.

claim: All isolated proteins electrophoresed as single species in non-denaturing PAGE.
source: All isolated proteins electrophoresed as single species in non-denaturing PAGE (lanes 1, 2, Figure 4A; lanes 1–4, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the gel images shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: When ReoM was incubated with PrkA-KD in the absence of ATP, a slower migrating species was observed corresponding to a ReoM:PrkA-KD complex.
source: When ReoM was incubated with PrkA-KD, in the absence of ATP, a slower migrating species was observed and the individual bands corresponding to ReoM and PrkA-KD disappeared indicating that the slower migrating species was a ReoM:PrkA-KD complex (lane 3, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the gel image shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When ReoM was incubated with PrkA-KD and Mg/ATP, a new species was present, migrating faster in the gel than ReoM, which is likely to be phosphorylated ReoM (P-ReoM).
source: When ReoM was incubated with PrkA-KD and Mg/ATP under the same conditions, free PrkA-KD was observed but no bands equivalent to ReoM and the ReoM:PrkA-KD complex remained; instead a new species was present, migrating faster in the gel than ReoM (lane 4, Figure 4A), which is likely to be phosphorylated ReoM (P-ReoM).
evidence: This is supported by the gel image shown in Figure 4A and the LC-MS data.

claim: LC-MS analysis of ReoM isolated from PrkA-KD after phosphorylation revealed the addition of 79.9 Da, corresponding to the formation of a singly-phosphorylated ReoM product.
source: Intact protein liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of ReoM isolated from PrkA-KD after phosphorylation revealed the addition of 79.9 Da in comparison to the mass of ReoM (10671.5 Da), which corresponds to the formation of a singly-phosphorylated ReoM product of 10751.4 Da (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the LC-MS data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MS/MS spectra were consistent with one phosphorylation event per protein chain.
source: MS/MS spectra obtained during peptide mass fingerprinting were also consistent with one phosphorylation event per protein chain
evidence: This is supported by the MS/MS data.

claim: Thr7 is the sole phosphosite in ReoM.
source: Analysis of the y- and b- ions in the MS/MS fragmentation spectrum of this peptide was consistent only with Thr7 as the sole phosphosite in ReoM (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the MS/MS data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutation of Thr7 to alanine completely abrogated the phosphorylation of ReoM by PrkA-KD.
source: Finally, mutation of Thr7 to alanine completely abrogated the phosphorylation of ReoM by PrkA-KD when analysed by LC-MS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the LC-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: No stable protein:protein complexes were formed between PrpC and either P-ReoM or PrkA-KD in the presence or absence of endogenous MnCl2.
source: Unlike the situation with ReoM and PrkA-KD, no stable protein:protein complexes were formed either in the presence or absence of endogenous MnCl2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the gel image shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The incubation of P-ReoM with PrpC and manganese resulted in the almost complete disappearance of the band corresponding to P-ReoM.
source: The incubation of P-ReoM with PrpC and manganese resulted in the almost complete disappearance of the band corresponding to P-ReoM (lane 6, Figure 4B) in comparison to the same reaction conducted without the addition of MnCl2 (lane 5, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the gel image shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of unphosphorylated ReoM and the absence of P-ReoM after PrpC treatment was confirmed by LC-MS.
source: The presence of unphosphorylated ReoM and the absence of P-ReoM was confirmed by LC-MS (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the LC-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: When incubated with PrpC in the presence of manganese ions, PrkA-KD had been dephosphorylated by PrpC.
